extracted.intended_audience: high school students preparing for the SAT (and their tutors/teachers)
extracted.subtask_description: Explaining the College Board SAT essay rubric and providing strategies to meet Reading, Analysis, and Writing criteria; guidance for writing and self-grading SAT-style argumentative analyses of a source text.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring procedure: graders and score scale
rubrics_metrics.description: Two graders each assign a score of 1-4 in Reading, Analysis, and Writing, producing a total essay score out of 8 in each area (two graders' scores combined).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If you don’t write on the assignment, plagiarize, or don't use your own original work, you'll get a 0 on your essay. Use the rubric as the framework graders use to assign the 1–4 scores in each category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures how well the response demonstrates comprehension of the source text and the author's argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Score descriptors (from College Board):
- 1 (Inadequate): little or no comprehension; fails to show understanding of central idea(s); may include only details without reference to central ideas; may contain numerous factual/interpretive errors; makes little or no use of textual evidence (quotations/paraphrases).
- 2 (Partial): some comprehension; shows understanding of central idea(s) but not important details; may contain errors; makes limited/haphazard use of textual evidence.
- 3 (Proficient): effective comprehension; shows understanding of central idea(s) and important details; free of substantive errors; makes appropriate use of textual evidence.
- 4 (Advanced): thorough comprehension; understands central idea(s) and how important details interrelate; free of errors; makes skillful use of textual evidence.
Guidance/strategy: Demonstrate factual accuracy (stick to what the text actually says; avoid misquoting or inaccurate paraphrase) and higher-level understanding (explain how details relate to central ideas and the structure of the author's argument). Use quotations or paraphrases correctly to show comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading — Surface Level: Factual Accuracy
rubrics_metrics.description: Staying faithful to what the passage actually says (no misstatements or contradictions) and correctly using the passage's facts when summarizing or quoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: paraphrasing the passage inaccurately (contradicting the text) undermines Reading score. Check direct quotations and paraphrases for fidelity to the passage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading — Higher Level: Understanding of Central Ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating an understanding of the passage's central idea(s) and how details and examples relate to and support that central idea.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explain relations between parts of the passage (e.g., how an analogy or example functions within the author's overall argument). Showing this interrelation helps you deconstruct how the author builds persuasiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Assesses how well the response analyzes the author's use of evidence, reasoning, and stylistic/persuasive elements to build an argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Score descriptors (from College Board):
- 1 (Inadequate): little or no analysis; identifies but does not explain elements of evidence/reasoning/style; analysis may be unwarranted; little or no support for claims; may be largely summary.
- 2 (Partial): limited analysis; attempts to describe author’s techniques but asserts without explaining importance; little or no support; may lack clear focus on relevant features.
- 3 (Proficient): effective analysis; competently evaluates the author’s techniques; contains relevant and sufficient support; focuses on features most relevant to the task.
- 4 (Advanced): insightful analysis; thorough, well-considered evaluation of the author's use of evidence/reasoning/style; contains relevant, sufficient, and strategically chosen support; consistently focuses on most relevant features.
Guidance/strategy: Analysis is the most important category — demonstrating critical reasoning about the author's argument and supporting that reasoning with textual evidence is essential for high scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis — Part I: Critical Thinking (Logic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating reasoning about the author's claim — evaluating how the argument works logically and making judgments based on analysis rather than summary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: merely asserting that the argument is 'persuasive' without explaining why. Good practice: explain the mechanics of persuasion (e.g., how analogies function to lead readers from a familiar premise to the author's claim). Showing reasoning (why a technique persuades) is necessary for higher Analysis scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Analysis — Part II: Examples, Reasons, and Other Evidence (Support)
rubrics_metrics.description: Backing up analytical claims with concrete, relevant support from the passage (quoted or paraphrased evidence) and choosing strategically relevant examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The rubric requires 'relevant, sufficient, and strategically chosen support' for claims. Anti-pattern: offering abstract reasoning without textual support. You have some leeway in interpreting effects on readers, but must provide convincing textual examples and explanations of their persuasive effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluates cohesion, control of language, clarity of a central claim, organization, sentence variety, precise word choice, and command of conventions of standard written English.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Score descriptors (from College Board):
- 1 (Inadequate): little or no cohesion; inadequate control of language; may lack clear central claim; lacks introduction/conclusion; poor progression of ideas; repetitive sentence structure; vague/poor word choice; weak control of conventions with numerous errors.
- 2 (Partial): limited cohesion; may lack/lose central claim; ineffective intro/conclusion; limited progression of ideas; limited sentence variety; general or repetitive word choice; limited control of conventions with errors that detract.
- 3 (Proficient): mostly cohesive; effective use/control of language; includes central claim (or implicit controlling idea); effective intro/conclusion; clear progression of ideas; sentence variety; some precise word choice; good control of conventions; free of significant errors.
- 4 (Advanced): cohesive and highly effective command of language; includes a precise central claim; skillful intro/conclusion; deliberate, highly effective progression of ideas; wide variety of sentence structures; consistent precise word choice; strong command of conventions; virtually free of errors.
Guidance/strategy: Be focused, organized, and precise; control conventions because persistent errors can interfere with meaning and lower scores.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing — Precise Central Claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Expressing a clear, specific thesis about how the author builds the argument (do not write vague or hedged theses).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid vague statements like 'There are a variety of ways the author builds his argument.' Instead specify the techniques you'll discuss (e.g., 'The author effectively builds his argument by using logic, allusions, and factual evidence'). You do not have to agree with the author's claim; focus on how the author persuades.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing — Organization
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating a deliberate and effective progression of ideas within and between paragraphs, including a recognizable introduction, body paragraphs, and conclusion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure your essay with an introduction (thesis), separate body paragraphs (one main example per paragraph is typical), and conclusion. Within each paragraph, connect each example to how it persuades the reader; avoid listing techniques without explaining their persuasive effect. Make your thesis clear in the opening paragraph so the grader can follow your reasoning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing — Vocab and Word Choice
rubrics_metrics.description: Using a wide, accurate, and precise vocabulary; word choice should be consistent and suited to a formal, objective tone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 4-scoring essay 'demonstrates a consistent use of precise word choice.' You are allowed occasional errors, but stick to words you know how to use correctly. Practice vocabulary in context and have knowledgeable reviewers check usage before using advanced words on test day.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing — Sentence Structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Demonstrating variety and clarity in sentence structures; avoid repetitive or awkward constructions that impede meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: multiple sentences beginning the same way, convoluted phrasing, or sentences that don't make sense. Good practice: vary sentence openings and constructions; revise awkward sentences; have others review practice essays to spot clunky phrasing. Longer essays often score higher, but sentence variety and clarity matter more than length alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Writing — Grammar, Punctuation, and Spelling (Conventions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Control of standard written English (grammar, punctuation, spelling) so errors do not interfere with meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Persistent errors that make the essay hard to understand will prevent top scores. Small quantities of mechanical errors may be overlooked. Proofread if time allows; if spelling is an issue, type and spellcheck practice essays to identify frequent mistakes. Ask a strong writer to review practice essays for errors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Textual Evidence (quotations and paraphrases)
rubrics_metrics.description: Incorporating appropriate quotations or paraphrases from the source text to support comprehension and analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher Reading and Analysis scores require 'appropriate' or 'skillful' use of textual evidence. Misquoting or badly paraphrasing weakens your essay. Use accurate quotations/paraphrases and explain how each piece of evidence functions within the author's argument.

rubrics_metrics.name: Application of the Rubric to Practice (self-grading and essay shaping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Using the rubric as a lens to plan essays and grade practice essays to identify weak areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use knowledge of what graders look for to shape thesis, organization, analysis, and evidence choices. When grading practice essays, apply rubric categories to find weaknesses (e.g., insufficient textual support, weak organization, grammar issues). Seek feedback from teachers/tutors or use services (e.g., PrepScholar platform) for custom grading and feedback.
